title: Semiconductor export controls: What chip smuggling reveals - I by IMD
body:
## Rapid read:

 The alleged Nvidia chip-smuggling case highlights how access to critical technologies is increasingly determined by geopolitics rather than price.
 Export controls have transformed advanced semiconductors from traded goods into strategically governed assets shaped by trust and national security.
 Companies and governments must strengthen compliance, verification, and supply-chain governance as access to key technologies becomes more restricted. [...] The United States also asked its allies to adopt similar controls. The Netherlands restricted ASML, the only maker of the most advanced chipmaking equipment, from servicing Chinese customers, and Japan placed similar limits on its own equipment makers. What began as one country’s national security policy became a coordinated, multinational system capable of reshaping access to critical technologies.

## Access decided by alignment, not by price [...] That changed with computing hardware. In 2019, the United States placed Huawei on its Entity List, restricting its access to American chips and chip design software. The shift accelerated in 2022 when Washington expanded controls beyond finished chips to include the equipment and software needed to design and manufacture them. For the first time, restrictions targeted an entire category of civilian technology and the ecosystem required to produce it.

title: Revamping Europe’s chips strategy: indispensability, not self-sufficiency
body: The rapidly growing strategic and economic significance of AI has turned the chip supply chain into a geopolitical asset. The US national security strategy now treats semiconductors as core security infrastructure6. In October 2022, a month before OpenAI released ChatGPT, Washington introduced export controls with the explicit objective of constraining Chinese AI development, framed as a matter of national security7. Europe is not a bystander in this contest: it has influence over several of [...] A sovereignty through indispensability strategy will also require instruments beyond industrial policy and the Chips Act 2. The EU needs to coordinate a coherent response to US and Chinese semiconductor policy. Export controls are of particular importance. The EU already has a Dual-Use Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2021/821) that harmonises export controls on chips and chip manufacturing equipment, but operational competence under the law remains national. [...] The European Commission now plans a Chips Act 2. The proposed revision1 must address the Chips Act’s shortcomings along with the new demands of the artificial-intelligence era and the shifting geopolitical reality that have emerged since it took effect. It remains necessary to reduce critical vulnerabilities but policy should not seek to replicate entire chip ecosystems in pursuit of self-sufficiency. Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted.

Perhaps not surprisingly, adversaries gained initial access via PHP2Shell, the collective name for two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The 9.2-severity-rated bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). [...] Products impacted by CVE-2026-123039 include Check Point’s Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms.

## Security tools are as big a target as what they protect [...] Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. They then escalated privileges to root using the CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

“Once attackers have root, they can run anything they like,” Dickson said. A management service on the appliance runs as root, listens on a local socket that any process on the box can write to, and never checks who is calling.

title: Microsoft just patched a serious Outlook flaw. Time to update! | PCWorld
body:
Credit: Microsoft

Microsoft has issued an urgent warning regarding an actively exploited security flaw in Outlook. Designated as CVE-2026-124194, the vulnerability enables attackers to trick users into opening a tampered message file. When opened, Outlook may connect to a server controlled by the attacker without displaying the usual security warning. This puts the user’s authentication credentials at risk of being leaked, which could lead to potential impersonation.

title: CVE-2026-119618: Critical Apache HTTP/2 RCE
body:
Successful exploitation should be treated as potential server compromise rather than simply a service crash. Investigators should look for new files, webshells, altered application code, persistence mechanisms, stolen credentials, suspicious outbound traffic, and evidence of lateral movement. [...] Successful exploitation can corrupt Apache’s heap and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. An attacker may execute commands using the privileges of the Apache process, potentially access sensitive application data, modify files, establish persistence, disrupt services, or use the compromised server as an entry point for further attacks. Red Hat assigns the flaw a generic CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

Can CVE-2026-119618 still affect me in 2026? [...] Anthropic’s OSS Scanner reported the issue to Apache’s security team on October 26, 2026 under identifier ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research independently reported the vulnerability on November 3. Apache released the fix on November 11.

The CVE record was published on November 11, 2026.

title: The geopolitics of AI and the rise of digital sovereignty | Brookings
body: While the United States takes a laissez-faire approach to regulating artificial intelligence, that tends to be fragmented at the state level, new industrial policy initiatives are aimed explicitly at strengthening certain aspects of the AI supply chain. One example is the CHIPS and Science Act, where Democrats and Republicans have come together to create new incentives for producing semiconductors on American soil.18 Based on the idea of digital sovereignty, the CHIPS and Science Act marks a [...] Concerning semiconductors, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the European Chips Act in February 2022, intending to make the EU a leader in semiconductor manufacturing.9 By 2030, the European share of global semiconductor production is expected to more than double, increasing from 9 to 20%. The European Chips Act is a response to the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act and China’s ambitions to achieve digital sovereignty through the development of semiconductors. Semiconductors [...] While the U.S. and the EU only recently have launched new initiatives and industrial policies explicitly aimed at semiconductors, China has long nurtured its chip industry.
